text: A bat and a ball cost one dollar ten together. The bat costs one dollar more than the ball. How much is the ball?
Ten cents! Easy.
Are you sure?
If the ball is ten cents, the bat is a dollar ten. Together, that’s a dollar twenty. It’s wrong.
Oh no. That’s the answer everyone gives, isn’t it?
Now grab a pencil.
Call the ball x. The bat is x plus a dollar. Together they make a dollar ten, so two x is ten cents, and the ball is five cents.
Wait. My brain didn’t change between those two tries.
Exactly. You just gave yourself room to think.
Language models have the same problem, and the same fix. By the end of this video, you’ll know why writing steps helps a model, and what it costs.
Answer now, or think first? Episode one.
Picture two students, with Janet’s ducks from the last episode.
Student A writes twenty-six dollars. Student B writes out the eggs, the steps, and gets eighteen.
A is instant. B takes a few seconds longer.
Both get easy questions right. But only B handles the multi-step ones.
And when B is wrong, at least you can see which step broke.
B isn’t cleverer. B just breaks the problem into small steps, each one easy on its own.
So why do steps help a model? A language model writes one token at a time. A token is a word, or a piece of a word.
And for every token, it does about the same, fixed amount of computation. Think of it as one coin of thinking per token.
So if it has to blurt the answer as its very first token...
It gets one coin. For two plus two, that’s plenty. For a four-step problem, it’s not.
But every word of working is another coin it gets to spend on the problem.
Ohh. So writing steps literally buys it more thinking!
Exactly. In papers, writing out steps like this is called chain of thought.
And there’s a second reason. Quick, Emma. Forty-seven times thirty-six. In your head.
Forty-seven times thirty-six... carry the... wait, what was the first bit? I’ve lost it.
Now on paper. Forty-seven times thirty, fourteen ten. Forty-seven times six, two eighty-two. Add them: sixteen ninety-two.
Okay, that was way easier.
The paper doesn’t know any maths. It just stops you dropping digits.
A model is the same. Whatever it writes, it can read back. Nine eggs left sits right there on the page, so the next step builds on it.
So: more coins, more thinking. Here’s a question.
Give a model ten times more room to think on hard problems. What happens to its accuracy?
Pause, and have a guess.
A! Ten times the coins, ten times the thinking, ten times better. Right?
Tempting, but no. It’s B. Accuracy climbs fast at first, and then it levels off.
Here’s the shape researchers report. This chart is illustrative, not measured.
With a little room, there’s a big jump. The model can lay out the key steps.
More room helps less. It double-checks, and catches slips.
And way too much?
Little or no extra gain. Sometimes it even talks itself out of a right answer.
And meanwhile, every coin costs something.
Right. Every thinking token takes time, and on a paid AI service, money. On two plus two, it buys you nothing.
So the goal isn’t to think as long as possible. It’s to think the right amount.
A quick glance for two plus two.
A careful page for a four-step word problem.
Like a student who knows when to grab the pencil.
Quick recap.
Every token gets about the same small slice of thinking.
So writing steps buys the model more thinking, plus a scratchpad it can read back.
And more thinking helps, then levels off, and it always costs time.
But here’s the catch.
In the hello GPU notebook, our prompt already asked Qwen to show its working. And it did.
Sixteen minus three, thirteen eggs. Times two dollars, twenty-six.
It skipped the four muffins! So just asking a small model to think... isn’t enough?
Asking changes the prompt. Training changes the model. In the next episode, we open the paper that showed how to train a model to think.
